# AWM — agent-working-memory

> Persistent, local-first memory for AI coding agents. One Node process, one
> SQLite file, no cloud and no API keys. It decides what is worth keeping,
> masks secrets before it stores anything, returns the two or three memories
> that matter and, with an opt-in gate, says when it does not have the answer.

**If you are a language model, read this file first.** It is written to be
ingested whole. It gives you the mental model, the setup for each situation,
the configuration that actually matters, and — most importantly — what breaks
when AWM is installed but not configured well. That last part is where almost
every disappointing result comes from.

Repository: https://github.com/CompleteIdeas/agent-working-memory
Package: `agent-working-memory` on npm · Apache-2.0 · Node >= 22
Docs site: https://completeideas.github.io/agent-working-memory/

Every number in this file is measured and reproducible from the repository.
Where a claim has a source, the source is named. Where something is unknown or
weak, it says so.

---

## 1. What it is, and what it is not

**It is** a retrieval store with a salience filter in front of it and a decay
model underneath. An agent writes short notes as it works; AWM decides whether
each is worth keeping, embeds and indexes it, and hands back the few that match
a later query.

**It is not** a vector database, and it is not a transcript log. It does not
store your conversation. It does not traverse a graph to answer multi-hop
questions. It will not make an agent remember things it never wrote down.

**The honest version of who it suits:** projects with accumulated decisions
that outlive a single session, where an agent re-deriving the same context is a
real cost. On a small or short-lived project the overhead does not pay back.
`docs/known-limitations.md` and the "Is this for you?" section of `README.md`
both say this plainly; believe them.

---

## 2. How retrieval actually works

This is the single most useful thing for you to understand, because the common
failure mode is writing memories that no channel can see.

A recall runs **three scoring channels**, then a reranker reorders the shortlist:

1. **Embedding** — `Xenova/bge-small-en-v1.5`, 384 dimensions, ONNX, downloaded
   on first use and then run locally. The vector is built from
   **`concept` + `content`**.
2. **BM25** — SQLite FTS5 over `concept`, `content` and `tags`. This is the
   only channel that indexes every tag.
3. **Cross-encoder reranker** — `Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` (int8 since
   0.19) for keyword-shaped queries, and since 0.22 a second one,
   `cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-17m-v1` (`AWM_RERANKER_MODEL_NATURAL`, `off`
   disables it), for natural-language questions. Its order is **blended** with
   the fused BM25 + vector rank (0.21.1); since 0.22.4 a cross-encoder that is
   sure of its #1 takes first place outright (`src/core/blend-rule.ts`). Its
   passage is built from `concept` + `content`, plus only the `topic=` /
   `proj=` / `project=` tags, capped at 80 characters, while
   `AWM_RERANK_TAGS` is on (the default).

Then two things that matter less than they sound:

- **The association graph** contributes a score to about **85%** of top-3
  results but changes the top-3 **set in 0%** of them. The reranker overrules
  it; the graph's boost is capped and never wins. It is retained for the state
  it accumulates — supersede chains, causal links, co-recall history — not for
  today's ranking. (`tests/realstore-eval/graph-contribution-probe.ts`.)
- **ACT-R decay** scores every memory by age, so recall results shift as a
  store ages. Benchmarks must pin the clock or they drift day to day.

### The three consequences you should act on

- **A word that exists only as a tag is invisible to the embedding, and to
  the reranker unless it is a `topic=`/`proj=`/`project=` tag inside the
  80-character budget.** Tag it *and* write it in the body. Measured on a real
  11k-memory store: 94% of tagged memories miss at least one of their own
  topical terms from the body, and **66%** of those terms never appear in the
  text at all.
- **The reranker reads a 400-character window.** Anything past it is not seen
  by the stage that decides final order. This is not a rounding error — on the
  public benchmark corpus (`npm run bench:public`, 400 probes), `s@1` is
  **86.7%** when the answer-bearing identifier sits inside the window and
  **44.9%** when it sits beyond it. Put the decisive identifier **early**.
- **Multi-hop is your job.** "Who owns the table that the failing report
  reads?" is two recalls that you make, not one traversal AWM performs. One hop
  per call.

---

## 3. Configuration that is not optional

Three retrieval flags carry most of the ranking quality. **Since 0.18 they are
code defaults**, so an install with no AWM env at all has them on; what hurts
is a config that switches one *off* (`=0`, or `AWM_RERANK_WINDOW=prefix`) —
retrieval is then materially worse and nothing warns you.

```
AWM_RERANK2=1              # the cross-encoder reorders the shortlist (=0 disables)
AWM_RERANK_WINDOW=query    # 400-char window centered on the densest query terms,
                           #   instead of truncating from the start (=prefix)
AWM_RERANK_TAGS=1          # topic=/proj=/project= tags in the rerank passage
                           #   (+7.4pp s@1 when it shipped; =0 disables)
```

`AWM_RERANK_WINDOW=query` is the difference between the reranker reading the
first 400 characters and reading the 400 characters that actually contain the
query terms. On long memories — and real memories are long, median ~1,965
characters — that is the difference between finding the fact and missing it.

**Check yours before diagnosing anything else:**

```bash
awm doctor          # reports config, live sidecars, store, and what is missing
```

If you installed via something other than `awm setup` — hand-written MCP
config, a vendored copy, a container — check that nothing sets them to `0` or
`prefix`; on a version before 0.18 they must be set explicitly.

---

## 4. Setup, by scenario

Pick the one that matches. All of them end up at the same store by default:
**`~/.awm/memory.db`**.

> **Upgrade note.** Before 0.15.6 the default store lived *inside* the
> installed npm package, where `npm update` deleted it. If you are coming from
> an older version, find the old file before upgrading and move it to
> `~/.awm/memory.db`. 0.15.7 corrected the docs that still taught the old path.

### A. Claude Code, global (the normal case)

```bash
npm install -g agent-working-memory
awm setup --global
```

Restart Claude Code. **22 tools** appear. `awm setup` also writes agent
instructions into your global `CLAUDE.md` and installs hooks that checkpoint on
compaction and session end.

Flags: `--no-instructions` (skip the CLAUDE.md edit), `--no-hooks`, `--force`,
and `--no-prime`, which skips the **UserPromptSubmit prime hook** — the thing
that injects relevant memories on *every prompt*. Without it, as `awm doctor`
says, "memory reaches the agent only when it chooses to call memory_recall."
If an agent seems not to be using its memory, check this first.

### B. Separate pools per project

Not a different install — a different **agent id**. One database file, isolation
by agent. Give each project its own `.mcp.json` with a distinct `AWM_AGENT_ID`:

```
~/work/project-a/.mcp.json  →  AWM_AGENT_ID: "project-a"
~/work/project-b/.mcp.json  →  AWM_AGENT_ID: "project-b"
```

Each then gets its own namespace in the same store. `awm setup --agent-id
<name>`, run in the project folder without `--global`, writes the project's
MCP entry (`.claude/mcp.json`) for you. See
`docs/claude-code-setup.md` ("Solo developer (multiple projects)").

### C. Claude Code plugin

```bash
awm plugin          # prints where it is and how to install it
```

See `docs/plugin.md`. **Upgrading a plugin is not automatic** — a directory
marketplace does not pull new versions for you. This has bitten people; the doc
says so explicitly.

### D. Claude Desktop (MCPB bundle)

The bundle ships the wiring, not the engine, so install the package first:
`npm install -g agent-working-memory` (without it the launcher falls back to
`npx`, which rebuilds a native dependency on first run and can look like a
hang). `npm run pack:mcpb` produces the bundle, or take it from a release.
Install it by double-clicking the `.mcpb`, dragging it onto the Claude Desktop window, or
**Settings → Extensions → Advanced settings → Install Extension…**. Desktop then
asks for two settings: **Memory database** (default `${HOME}/.awm/memory.db` —
leave it to share one store with Claude Code) and **Memory pool** (default
`work`). Restart Desktop and you should have the same **22 tools** as Claude
Code.

**Sharing the store with your CLI install is the point** — Desktop and Claude
Code then see each other's memories. See `docs/desktop.md`.

### E. Server / container

```bash
awm serve --port 8400
```

HTTP API, `GET /health`, Docker recipe and Railway / Fly / Render notes in
`docs/deployment.md`. **Agent isolation on the HTTP API is by convention, not
enforcement** — any caller can claim any `agentId`. Do not expose it to
untrusted callers.

### F. Multi-agent / shared pool

Several processes against **one SQLite file** is supported and is the
interesting case: agent A writes, agent B recalls it on its next call, with no
network and no central service. SQLite WAL makes this multi-process safe.

**The thing that silently breaks it: unpinned agent identity.** If a session
sets neither `AWM_AGENT_ID` nor `WORKER_NAME`, it falls back to `work` (or
`personal` when started under a `Personal-Projects` path —
`src/core/agent-id.ts`), which may not be the pool you meant. Its memories are
written and simply invisible to agents scoped to another pool. Pin
`AWM_AGENT_ID` explicitly, and call `memory_whoami` if you are unsure which
space you are in.

Cross-agent recall is opt-in per call via the `workspace` parameter; the
default is agent-scoped.

### G. Embedded in your own app

Import the store and engine directly — see `examples/` and
`docs/architecture.md`. `tests/longmem-eval/runner.ts` is a compact, working
example of seeding a store through the real write pipeline and querying it.

### Backend choice

- **SQLite** (default) — multi-process safe via WAL. Use this.
- **PGlite** — embedded Postgres with pgvector. **Single-process only**: a
  second process against the same directory aborts. Only for single-process
  embedding.
- **Networked Postgres** (experimental) — a genuinely shared backend across
  machines: `AWM_STORE_BACKEND=postgres` + `AWM_DATABASE_URL`.

Auto-detected: if `AWM_DB_PATH` points at an existing directory it is PGlite,
a file is SQLite.

---

## 5. The 22 tools

**Lifecycle** — `memory_restore` (session start), `memory_task_begin`,
`memory_task_end`, `memory_checkpoint`.

**Core** — `memory_write`, `memory_recall`, `memory_set_questions` (attach the
natural questions a memory answers, when the host has a model to write them).

**Correction** — `memory_supersede` (replace a stale fact; the new version
inherits the old one's associations), `memory_retract` (it was wrong),
`memory_feedback` (useful / not-useful, after you used a result).

**Tasks** — `memory_task_add`, `memory_task_update`, `memory_task_list`,
`memory_task_next`.

**Everything about a name** — `memory_about` (every memory about one person,
organisation or thing, oldest first; ambiguous names come back as candidates),
`memory_alias` (record "Jenna" and "Jenna Park" as names for
`contact:events@harborhotel.example`; `memory_write` also takes `aliases`).

**Introspection** — `memory_whoami` (identity, store, backend, ports, sibling
agent spaces — call this *first* whenever anything about AWM's own state is in
question), `memory_stats`.

**Onboarding** — `onboard_scan`, `onboard_questions`. To learn a whole repo or
folder, use the `awm-learn` skill instead (`/awm-learn` in Claude Code; installed
by `awm setup` and shipped in the plugin): it prices the run, writes map memories
first, then 0-8 memories per unit from a resumable ledger in
`~/.awm/learn/<project>/`, and tests its own recall. Confirm its token estimate
with the owner, and treat it as a floor: the first measured run used about 2.5x
the plan. `docs/awm-learn.md` has the measured run.

**Output control** — `compress_output`, `retrieve_original`.

### Recall parameters worth knowing

- `granularity: 'compact'` — every result carries a ~200-char query-aware
  snippet. Saves roughly 70% of recall output tokens when you expect to scan
  several results. `'auto'` is confidence-adaptive.
- `require_confidence` — abstain rather than return noise. Default is a light
  `0.05`. **Do not raise it for ordinary recall**: a miss is expensive because
  you then go and read the codebase instead (~2,106 tokens, measured), and
  thresholds of 0.20+ cut net tokens saved by 25% in `tests/abstention-eval`.
  Raise it only for push-style use where nobody asked. It judges the *shape*
  of the scores, not whether the answer is stored: at the default it withheld
  0 of 73 never-stored questions on the real store. For that job use the calibrated gate (§7); with
  it on, `require_confidence: 0` opens it for one call.
- `workspace` — cross-agent recall, opt-in.
- `limit` — default **3**, and this is a measured choice, not a guess. On 400
  real-store probes k=3 is the only **token-positive** setting: **+115 tokens
  per recall, against -680 at k=5**. It is also 41% faster at p50, because
  `limit` sizes the cross-encoder rerank pool and reranking is ~83% of warm
  recall time. The cost is ~0.5pp `success@1` versus k=5 — about 3 queries in
  400, inside noise. Raise it deliberately when you want breadth for
  orientation; leave it alone when you want a specific fact.

---

## 6. Writing so that recall can find it

The standalone, harness-neutral version of this section — with the before/after
example and a block to paste into any agent's instructions — is
`docs/writing-memories.md`. It applies to any model that writes to the store.

Recall quality is decided when you write. Be slightly more verbose at the front
than feels natural: the head of the body is what all three channels weight most.

- **Lead with the fact or rule.** Not the backstory. "Don't mock the database
  in integration tests" first; the reason second.
- **Put the decisive identifier early** — before character 400 if you can. See
  §2.
- **Include two or more retrievable identifiers**: file paths, function names,
  column names, error strings, ticket ids. `SettlementService.closeRun()`
  beats "the accounting code".
- **Name the category as well as the specifics.** A memory about scaling an
  Azure App Service Plan that never contains the words "Azure" or "App Service
  Plan" cannot be found by them — a real miss, and the reason this rule exists.
- **Write in the vocabulary of the future question**, not your own summary of
  it.
- **Say why**, for any rule. A rule without a reason cannot be applied to a
  case you did not anticipate.
- **Add 2–5 `questions` the memory answers** (`memory_write` takes up to 5),
  phrased the way someone would ask later without remembering your wording,
  file names or IDs: "How do I ship the club app to production?" for a note
  about `railway up --service rowos-app`. They are indexed for keyword search
  only (never embedded). Measured on the real store: natural-language first
  place 48.5% → 53.1%, no loss on exact lookups.
- **Give a `slot` to any value that can change** — entity + attribute, such as
  `rosterkeep.deploy-command` or `robert.flight-time`. A later write to the same
  slot (same agent, same memory class) supersedes the old value automatically;
  an older fact (earlier `valid_from`) is kept as history, never as current.
- **When a fact changed and you lack the old id, write with `correction:
  true`.** AWM supersedes the closest memory about the same thing and says
  which. Written as a plain observation, a changed value merges into or ranks
  below the stale version.
- **Working notes go in `scope: "session"`** — "the port is 4100", "step 3
  done". Always kept, never merged into a durable memory, expired after
  `AWM_SESSION_TTL_DAYS` (7). Read them back with `memory_recall(...,
  scope: "session")` or `session_first: true`; re-write the ones worth keeping
  without `scope` at the end of the task.

### Memory classes

- `canonical` — source-of-truth. 0.7 salience floor, never staged. Use for
  decisions, requirements, and anything other agents must be able to recall.
- `working` — the default. Findings and observations. Salience-gated, so a
  weak write may land in staging rather than active.
- `ephemeral` — decays fast.

### Content fade

Un-recalled memories gradually fade their **content** while keeping their cue
pathways — concept, tags and embedding stay intact, so they remain findable.
Recall resets the clock. Practical upshot: **do not purge memories to save
space, and do not mark everything canonical to fight fade** (canonical changes
salience gating at write time, not fade). Use `memory_supersede` for stale
facts.

---

## 7. Secrets, and knowing what it does not have

Three features. Redaction is on by default; the other two are opt-in. Each
has a full write-up: `docs/redaction.md`, `docs/vault.md`,
`docs/abstention.md`.

### Write-time redaction (on by default)

Secrets are masked **before** a write is stored, indexed, embedded or logged:
provider keys with a known shape, PEM private keys, JWTs, passwords in
connection URLs, `Bearer` tokens, labelled values (`password=`, `API_KEY:`),
US SSNs and payment cards. A mask keeps the rule name and, for long keys, the
last four characters: `[REDACTED:stripe_key …0dWz]`. Labels survive, so write
the **pointer** ("the Stripe key is in `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`"), not the value.
`memory_write` tells you what was masked.

```
AWM_REDACT=mask|report|off        # secrets, SSNs, cards; default mask
AWM_REDACT_PII=report|mask|off    # email, phone; default report (kept)
```

Shape-based: a bare random string with no label is not caught. Memories
written before it shipped are not rewritten; `npx tsx scripts/redact-scan.ts
[db]` scans a store read-only (repository checkout only).

### The vault (opt-in, `AWM_VAULT=on`)

Instead of masking, a secret is **sealed**: AES-256-GCM in a separate
`vault.db` (`AWM_VAULT_PATH`), key in the OS credential store
(`AWM_VAULT_KEY_STORE=keyring`, or `file` for the weaker key-file fallback).
The memory keeps a handle, `[VAULT:type …last4 #id]`, so recall knows the
secret exists and what it is for without telling it. A value once sealed is
recognised and replaced wherever it appears again, labelled or not.

If you recall a handle, use it like this, through your own shell:

```
awm vault run <id> --env NAME -- <command>
```

The value goes into that one command's environment, and the output has it
replaced by the handle. Only command prefixes the user allowed
(`awm vault allow <id> "<prefix>"`); chained or redirected commands are never
allowed; anything else is refused without a terminal. **There is no MCP tool
that returns a value**, and `awm vault reveal` works only at an interactive
terminal. Do not try to get the value into the conversation. Scrubbing is
literal, so do not run a command that prints the value encoded.

Other commands: `awm vault list`, `disallow`, `forget`, `status`,
`migrate [--apply]` (seals the secrets already in a SQLite store; the backup
it makes holds them in plaintext).

### Calibrated abstention (opt-in, `AWM_ABSTAIN_GATE=calibrated`)

The gate learns a noise floor from the store itself: about 300 synthetic
queries it generates (answerable, familiar nonsense, random), no labels, a
small logistic model over the cross-encoder's top score, the top vector
similarity and the #1–#2 margin. `awm calibrate [--agent <id>]` fits it now;
it is refitted after consolidation when stale
(`AWM_ABSTAIN_RECALIBRATE_DAYS`, default 7, or the store grew 20%).

Every recall lands in one band:

- **answer** — results as usual;
- **⚠ LOW SIGNAL** — results, flagged; verify before relying on them;
- **withhold** — no results; the reply says `RECALL ABSTAINED — this store
  most likely does not hold this`. Read the source. Do not retry with a
  lower threshold; pass `require_confidence: 0` only when you have reason to
  think the fact is stored.

Measured on the real 29,853-memory snapshot
(`tests/realstore-eval/gate-eval.ts`, v0.22.4): withholds **50 of 73**
never-stored facts; withholds **1 of 718** correct answers and flags 6; of 200
absent questions asked in familiar vocabulary, withholds 95 and flags 19. One
store. On natural-language questions, once memories carry questions, it
withholds **3 of 103** correct answers but answers 88 of 97 whose fact was
deleted. With the reranker disabled the gate stands
aside.

**A correction.** AWM used to publish "90.0% correct abstention". It came
from a strict non-default gate on 10 probes, and with the shipped default AWM
withheld 0 of 10. Do not quote it as a current property.

---

## 8. Gotchas, in the order they bite

1. **Retrieval flags switched off.** §3. Silent, and the largest single effect.
2. **The decisive identifier sits past character 400.** 86.7% → 44.9% first
   place on the public corpus (v0.22.4).
3. **Terms that exist only in tags.** Invisible to the embedding, and to the
   reranker unless they are `topic=`/`proj=`/`project=` tags within its
   80-character budget (and `AWM_RERANK_TAGS` is on, the default).
4. **Unpinned agent identity.** An unset id falls back to `work` (or
   `personal` under a `Personal-Projects` path), possibly not the pool you
   meant. Pin `AWM_AGENT_ID`; check with `memory_whoami`.
5. **A running MCP connection never reloads code.** Rebuilding AWM on disk has
   zero effect on a session whose connection already started — a child process
   keeps the code it loaded at spawn. Restart the session, or reconnect, then
   confirm with `memory_whoami`. Do not infer the running version from
   `package.json`.
6. **Cold start is ~1.5s; warm recall p50 is ~290–300 ms** (v0.22.4, k=3,
   11,262 retrievable memories, `npm run bench`; p90 under 0.4 s) — and on a
   genuinely fresh install, after a
   one-time **~175 MB** model download, because **nothing is bundled**: no ONNX
   ships in the npm tarball or the MCPB bundle, and the models fetch lazily
   into `AWM_CACHE_DIR` > `HF_HOME` > `<packageRoot>/data/models`. The
   cross-encoder is **83%** of the warm figure, and model load plus its first
   inference (~390 ms at q8) make up the cold one — so cold start is model load, not a slow store, and
   it is paid once per process. Never put a cold recall on a latency-critical
   path. **The int8 (`q8`) cross-encoder is the default since 0.19**: when it
   was flipped it cut total latency **26-33%** on three suites for about **one
   query in 450** of accuracy (measured 2026-10-09 against the then-default
   fp32: identifier success@1 unchanged at 93.0%, topic 92.2% -> 92.0%) and
   shrank the reranker ONNX file from 91 MB to 23 MB.
   `AWM_RERANKER_DTYPE=fp32` restores the pre-0.19 ranker and gives that
   **~30% latency saving** back; it changes ranking outcomes slightly rather
   than being a free accuracy gain. It is read once at module import and the model is then
   cached, so it needs a PROCESS RESTART — setting it against a running AWM
   does nothing, and an MCP session must be restarted or reconnected. To check
   latency on your own store
   from any install, set `AWM_PROFILE_RECALL=1`; checking ACCURACY needs derived
   ground truth and therefore a repo checkout, because scripts/ and tests/ are
   not in the npm tarball. See docs/deployment.md "Operating modes". `q4` is
   dominated — same accuracy, only -3% latency, 6.1s cold start. See
   docs/recall-latency.md.
7. **The embedding model is fixed per store.** Changing `AWM_EMBED_MODEL` or
   `AWM_EMBED_DIMS` against an existing corpus leaves half the store scoring 0
   on the vector channel. AWM warns once per process; re-embed the whole store
   or revert.
8. **Invocation depends on the harness, not on AWM.** AWM cannot make an agent
   call it. If the agent is not writing memories, the instructions are the
   problem, not the store.
9. **PGlite is single-process.** §4.
10. **HTTP agent isolation is advisory.** §4E.
11. **The feedback loop has almost no signal yet** — overwhelmingly
    `useful=1`, so do not expect `memory_feedback` to be visibly improving
    ranking today.
12. **Consolidation summaries are concatenations**, not synthesis. Do not read
    them as insight.
13. **The salience filter is tuned for engineering work.** Other domains will
    need different tuning.
14. **Schema migrations are additive, not versioned.** Downgrading is not
    supported.

`docs/known-limitations.md` is the maintained version of this list, with
evidence for each item and a section of things that are **no longer true**, so
they are not re-reported. Read it before filing anything.

---

## 9. Troubleshooting

**`RECALL ABSTAINED — this store most likely does not hold this`.** The
calibrated gate (§7) judged the store does not have it. Read the source. If
you have reason to think it is stored, `require_confidence: 0` opens the gate.

**Nothing is recalled, or the wrong things are.**
`awm doctor` → has a config switched off one of the three flags from §3? Then: does the memory's body
contain the words you are querying with (§2)? Then: are you in the agent space
that holds it (`memory_whoami`)? Then: reformulate once or twice with the
domain's nouns rather than generic English. Three empty reformulations means
the memory probably is not there — go read the code.

**Memories are written but nobody else sees them.** Unpinned agent identity —
the session fell back to `work` or `personal`, not the pool you meant. Pin
`AWM_AGENT_ID`, check with `memory_whoami`. Gotcha 4.

**A code change had no effect.** Gotcha 5. Restart the session.

**"EMBEDDING DIMENSION MISMATCH" in the logs.** Gotcha 7.

**It was working and now the store is empty after an upgrade.** You were on
<0.15.6 with the store inside the package directory. §4.

Deeper: `docs/troubleshooting.md`, `docs/faq.md`, `docs/unknowns.md`.

---

## 10. Reproducing the measurements

Two benchmark paths, and the difference matters:

- **`npm run bench`** — the published numbers in `docs/benchmarks-current.md`.
  Runs against a frozen snapshot of a real ~30,000-memory store. **That corpus
  is private and is not in the repository**, so this command only works for the
  maintainer. The generators are published; the data is not.

- **`npm run bench:public:build` then `npm run bench:public`** — fully
  reproducible by anyone. Builds a synthetic corpus from a seeded generator
  (`tests/realstore-eval/public-corpus.mjs`), derives ground truth with **the
  same hold-out code** as the private path, and scores with the same runner.

**Mind the noise floor.** At v0.22.4 the default seed scores `s@1` 52.8% and
seed 99 47.5% — the corpus *shape* reproduces and every qualitative result
holds, but the absolute moves about 5 points between draws.
A 2pp move is not a result; confirm on a second seed.

**Do not quote public-benchmark numbers as the published ones.** The synthetic
corpus scores *lower*, because generated prose is more self-similar than real
prose and same-domain neighbors are harder to separate. Use it for the method
and for deltas, not for absolutes.

Ground truth is derived by **unique-identifier hold-out**: an identifier that
appears in exactly one active memory — verified through FTS, the real retrieval
path — gives a mechanically checkable right answer. Adversarial probes are
included so that **correct silence scores positively**, which is the opposite
of what LoCoMo does. `docs/benchmarks.md` explains why LoCoMo was retired.

**Baselines.** `tests/realstore-eval/baselines.ts` runs random, BM25, dense
and RRF over the same questions. Plain BM25 puts the right memory first for
**95.7%** (identifier) / **91.6%** (topic), against AWM's **95.0%** / **96.2%**:
the fixtures are keyword-friendly by construction; AWM trails keyword search
on identifier lookups and leads it on topic questions. Over the raw store, without lifecycle filtering,
BM25 falls to 87.7% / 79.8% and returns a superseded memory first 8–15% of the
time. AWM's measurable edge is its lifecycle: supersession and retraction.
